title: Benedict Joseph Labre (1748–1783)
hook: rejected by monasteries, he lived as a holy beggar on the streets of Rome

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Carmelites of Compiègne, who sang Laudate Dominum on their way to the guillotine. Your line was singing to the scaffold. Today, a saint the crowds walked past.

Night in Rome, among the broken arches of the Colosseum. In a niche in the stone, a man in rags is asleep. His coat is torn, his hair matted, a rosary hangs around his neck, and in a small sack he carries a few prayer books and not much else. By day you'll find him in the city's churches, kneeling very still for hours before the Blessed Sacrament. People step around him. Some hold their noses. A few drop a coin, and tradition says he often gives it away to someone poorer. His name is Benedict Joseph Labre.
screen: `ASLEEP IN THE COLOSSEUM.` → `KNEELING FOR HOURS.` → `PEOPLE STEP AROUND HIM.`

segments.voice: First, the doors that closed. Benedict Joseph grew up in northern France and wanted one thing: to be a monk. He knocked at Carthusian houses and Trappist monasteries. He was turned away, or taken in and then fell ill and had to leave. Again and again, the door he was sure God wanted kept closing. Second, the road. So he stopped knocking and started walking. He became a pilgrim, going on foot from shrine to shrine across Europe, sleeping outdoors, begging only what he needed for the day. He said little. He prayed constantly. Third, Rome. In the end he stayed in Rome, sleeping in the ruins and spending his days in its churches. He looked like what he was: a homeless man. Some called him a madman or a fraud. Jesus said of himself, in Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air nests: but the son of man hath not where to lay his head." Labre took that line and lived inside it. Fourth, the saint is dead. During Holy Week he collapsed near a church and was carried into a nearby house, where he died. Tradition says children ran through the streets crying, the saint is dead. People who had stepped around him came to his funeral. The Church later declared him a saint. Some Catholics read him alongside Matthew twenty-five, where Jesus says: "I was a stranger, and you took me in." In that reading, Labre was the stranger.
screen: `THE MONASTERY DOORS CLOSE.` · `A PILGRIM ON FOOT.` · `A HOMELESS MAN IN ROME.` · `THE SAINT IS DEAD.` · then, large: `I WAS A STRANGER, AND YOU TOOK ME IN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone without a home you've passed recently, at a station, outside a shop, on a bench, and try to remember their face, not just their sign or their bags. Hold them as a person with a story you haven't heard, and decide one small thing for next time: eye contact, a greeting, asking their name. If you pray, hold them before God.
Pilgrim. What Benedict Joseph Labre became after monasteries turned him away: a beggar walking from shrine to shrine, sleeping outdoors, praying constantly.
Your line: the holy beggar. The man people stepped around was the one the children called a saint. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics who serve people experiencing homelessness sometimes invoke Saint Benedict Joseph Labre, and his relics and tomb are kept in the church of Santa Maria ai Monti in Rome, near where he died.

chat.says: Why would the Church make a homeless beggar a saint?
options: He was a pilgrim who prayed constantly and owned almost nothing.
Because he secretly came from a rich family and gave it all up.
Because crowds followed him around Rome to watch his miracles.
chat.meaning: Turned away by monasteries, Labre walked from shrine to shrine, prayed for hours and, tradition says, gave his coins away; people stepped around him, then called him a saint.

Colosseum.meaning: the ancient arena in Rome, now in ruins

Benedict Joseph Labre.meaning: a French pilgrim who lived as a beggar in Rome

Carthusian.meaning: an order of monks whose houses turned him away

Trappist.meaning: another order of monks whose doors closed to him

notes: Claims rule: no dates, ages or counts spoken (his age at death and the number of monasteries are left out). Confirm.
Carthusian and Trappist attempts, and his brief stay at Sept-Fons ending in illness, summarized as 'turned away, or taken in and then fell ill'. Confirm.
Sleeping in the Colosseum ruins, giving away alms, and children crying 'the saint is dead' are traditional; the last is attributed to tradition. Confirm.
Death in Holy Week near Santa Maria ai Monti, carried into a nearby house (traditionally a butcher's): confirm.
Greek ξένος in Matthew 25:35 (ξένος ἤμην): confirm.
